Risky/removed Chrome ad-block extension IDs present on endpoint (Island 'Adblock for YouTube' set) AIInstallation High
Hunts for the on-disk presence of the specific Chrome extension IDs Island flagged: 'Adblock for YouTube' (cmedhionkhpnakcndndgjdbohmhepckk, dormant trusted-create-element script-injection capability) plus three related ad blockers already pulled from the Web Store for malware. Detection is article-specific because it pins the exact extension folder IDs, not a generic 'browser extension' template. Rationale: Uses the four concrete Chrome extension IDs named in the article (the flagged cmedhionkhpnakcndndgjdbohmhepckk plus onomjaelhagjjojbkcafidnepbfkpnee / ogcaehilgakehloljjmajoempaflmdci / gekoepiplklhniacchbbgbhilidiojmb, all removed for malware). IDs are immutable Chrome identifiers, so file-path matches are deterministic. Extension ID corroborated via Extpose and CRXcavator listings. Cross-checked against: • https://extpose.com/ext/cmedhionkhpnakcndndgjdbohmhepckk • https://crxcavator.io/report/cmedhionkhpnakcndndgjdbohmhepckk?platform=Chrome • https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/adblock-for-youtube/cmedhionkhpnakcndndgjdbohmhepckk
ATT&CKT1176 T1185
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User genuinely installed the still-listed 'Adblock for YouTube' (10M+ installs) for its advertised function — presence is not compromise
  • Corporate-approved or GPO-pushed ad blocker that happens to be one of these IDs
  • Chrome profile sync replicating the extension folder across a user's enrolled devices
  • Security researcher detonating the extension in an analysis sandbox
  • Leftover orphaned extension folder from a prior install that was never cleaned up
Suppression filter
// Promote to alerting only for the storefront-removed (confirmed-malware) IDs; treat the 10M-install one as inventory:
| where MatchedExtId in ("onomjaelhagjjojbkcafidnepbfkpnee","ogcaehilgakehloljjmajoempaflmdci","gekoepiplklhniacchbbgbhilidiojmb")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm which ID matched. The three removed-for-malware IDs (onomjaelhagjjojbkcafidnepbfkpnee, ogcaehilgakehloljjmajoempaflmdci, gekoepiplklhniacchbbgbhilidiojmb) are unambiguous — treat as malicious. For cmedhionkhpnakcndndgjdbohmhepckk, note version and check the manifest permissions (all-urls / scripting). 2) Contain: force-remove via Chrome ExtensionInstallBlocklist / ExtensionInstallForcelist policy and uninstall the extension; rotate creds for any sensitive web sessions used on that host (banking, admin panels, work SaaS). 3) Hunt: pivot to UC2 (network beacons to api.adblock-for-youtube.com) on the same host, and sweep the fleet for all four IDs to size exposure.
let extIds = dynamic(["cmedhionkhpnakcndndgjdbohmhepckk","onomjaelhagjjojbkcafidnepbfkpnee","ogcaehilgakehloljjmajoempaflmdci","gekoepiplklhniacchbbgbhilidiojmb"]);
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has_any (extIds)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe","chrome_proxy.exe","opera.exe")
| extend MatchedExtId = extract(@"(cmedhionkhpnakcndndgjdbohmhepckk|onomjaelhagjjojbkcafidnepbfkpnee|ogcaehilgakehloljjmajoempaflmdci|gekoepiplklhniacchbbgbhilidiojmb)", 1, FolderPath)
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), FileWrites=count(), SampleFolder=any(FolderPath) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, MatchedExtId
| order by LastSeen desc
let extIds = dynamic(["cmedhionkhpnakcndndgjdbohmhepckk","onomjaelhagjjojbkcafidnepbfkpnee","ogcaehilgakehloljjmajoempaflmdci","gekoepiplklhniacchbbgbhilidiojmb"]);
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has_any (extIds)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| extend MatchedExtId = extract(@"(cmedhionkhpnakcndndgjdbohmhepckk|onomjaelhagjjojbkcafidnepbfkpnee|ogcaehilgakehloljjmajoempaflmdci|gekoepiplklhniacchbbgbhilidiojmb)", 1, TargetFilePath)
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), FileWrites=count(), SampleFolder=any(TargetFilePath) by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, MatchedExtId
| order by LastSeen desc

Browser beacon to Adblock for YouTube config/activation backend (api.adblock-for-youtube.com) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts for browser-initiated network/DNS traffic to api.adblock-for-youtube.com, the server-side endpoint that fetches the extension's scriptlet configuration. Island's whole thesis is that a single config response can flip the dormant 'trusted-create-element' rule into live arbitrary-JS injection — so this channel is the activation surface worth watching. Article-specific because it pins the extension's exact backend host. Rationale: Pivots on api.adblock-for-youtube.com, the article's named extension backend that fetches scriptlet config (the trusted-create-element activation path). Domain is single-sourced (original article/IOC bundle only) so confidence is Medium; it cleanly maps to the extension's own name, lowering hallucination risk, but a second-source confirmation was not found. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/chrome-ad-blocker-with-10m-installs.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1102 T1059.007
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimately installed extension performing its normal config/update poll to its own backend
  • Corporate proxy or DNS resolver logging the lookup on behalf of many clients (source IP = proxy, not real host)
  • Threat-intel or URL-scanning sandbox resolving the domain during analysis
  • Browser prefetch/DNS pre-resolution speculatively resolving the host without a real request
  • Security tooling (EDR/secure web gateway) actively probing the domain for categorization
Suppression filter
// Reduce proxy/aggregator noise by requiring the lookup to originate from a browser process on a real endpoint (Defender variant):
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process/host and confirm it correlates with an on-disk extension hit from UC1; pull the actual HTTP transaction (URI, response size) from the web-proxy if available to see if a config payload was served. 2) Contain: block api.adblock-for-youtube.com at the secure web gateway/DNS sinkhole and force-remove the extension via Chrome policy on affected hosts. 3) Hunt: inspect served config responses for the 'trusted-create-element' scriptlet rule or injected <script> directives; review browser session activity to sensitive web apps (admin panels, mail, banking) for the affected users around the beacon window.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "adblock-for-youtube.com"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Connections=count(), Hosts=dcount(DeviceName), RemoteIPs=make_set(RemoteIP, 10) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteUrl
| order by LastSeen desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has "adblock-for-youtube.com"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Queries=count() by SrcIpAddr, DvcHostname, DnsQuery
| order by LastSeen desc

New Gaslight macOS Malware Uses Prompt Injection to Disrupt AI-Assisted Analysis

The Hacker News
2026-06-25 8 use cases 2 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

A previously undocumented Rust-based macOS implant and information stealer has been found to embed a prompt injection payload designed to trick a malware analyst's artificial intelligence (AI) tools and trick it into aborting or refusing an analysis of the artifact. The malware has been codenamed Gaslight owing to this deceptive behavior. It's been assessed with high confidence that the tool is

ATT&CKT1190 T1555.003

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Gaslight macOS LaunchAgent persistence spoofing 'com.apple.system.services.activity' · [LLM] Gaslight standalone CPython 3.10.18 interpreter staged from python-build-standalone · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Gaslight Telegram Bot API getUpdates C2 polling from non-browser macOS process · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Gaslight collection archive temp/collected_data.zip staged for Telegram exfiltration · [LLM] Gaslight credential theft: macOS keychain + Chrome/Brave/Firefox/Safari store access · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Gaslight macOS LaunchAgent persistence spoofing 'com.apple.system.services.activity' AIInstallation High
Hunts the specific LaunchAgent Gaslight drops for persistence: a .plist labelled com.apple.system.services.activity written into a user LaunchAgents directory and pointing at a non-Apple binary. Legitimate Apple services never install a com.apple.* agent into ~/Library/LaunchAgents, so this label-in-user-scope pairing is high fidelity. Rationale: Uses the exact persistence label 'com.apple.system.services.activity' and the ~/Library/LaunchAgents scope from the article; corroborated by SentinelOne (which adds that the plist's ProgramArguments resolves the implant's own path via __NSGetExecutablePath) and Infosecurity Magazine. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/labs/macos-gaslight-rust-backdoor-turns-prompt-injection-on-the-analyst-not-the-sandbox/ • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/macos-gaslight-rust-backdoor/
ATT&CKT1543.001 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate MDM/EDR tool that incorrectly names its agent under a com.apple.* label (rare; check signing)
  • Internal IT scripts deploying user LaunchAgents with copied Apple-style labels
  • Security researcher reproducing the sample in a test VM
  • Backup/restore tooling rewriting an existing LaunchAgents directory
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "/System/" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "/usr/libexec/"
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the plist's ProgramArguments — a non-Apple, ad-hoc-signed or user-writable binary path (e.g. in /Users, /tmp, /private/var) confirms malice; a genuine Apple binary in /System would be benign. 2) Contain: unload the agent (launchctl bootout) and quarantine the referenced binary; isolate the host from the network to break Telegram C2. 3) Hunt: pivot on the binary hash across the fleet, then look for the cpython-3.10.18 staging, temp/collected_data.zip, and api.telegram.org egress on the same host.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has "/Library/LaunchAgents/"
| where FileName =~ "com.apple.system.services.activity.plist" or FolderPath has "com.apple.system.services.activity"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("launchd","cfprefsd","installer","Installer")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has "/Library/LaunchAgents/"
| where TargetFileName =~ "com.apple.system.services.activity.plist" or TargetFilePath has "com.apple.system.services.activity"
| where ActingProcessName !has "launchd" and ActingProcessName !has "cfprefsd"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Gaslight standalone CPython 3.10.18 interpreter staged from python-build-standalone AIInstallation High
Hunts Gaslight's self-staged Python theft environment: a Base64 bash installer drops a cpython-3.10.18 interpreter from the astral-sh/python-build-standalone project and runs it. The unique 'cpython-3.10.18' / 'python-build-standalone' path tokens make a non-developer host running this interpreter highly suspicious. Rationale: Pivots on the article's exact 'cpython-3.10.18' interpreter version and 'astral-sh/python-build-standalone' source; SentinelOne and Arabian Post both confirm the runtime-fetched standalone CPython staging chain. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/labs/macos-gaslight-rust-backdoor-turns-prompt-injection-on-the-analyst-not-the-sandbox/ • https://thearabianpost.com/gaslight-malware-exposes-ai-triage-blind-spot/
ATT&CKT1059.006 T1059.004 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developers using uv/rye/astral toolchains that legitimately fetch python-build-standalone CPython builds
  • CI/CD agents or Homebrew formulae bootstrapping a pinned 3.10.18 runtime
  • Data-science users with portable Python environments
  • Penetration-test or detection-validation activity replaying the sample
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "/.local/" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "/.cache/" and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("uv","rye","brew")
Response runbook
1) Triage: check the parent process and the install location — a cpython-3.10.18 dropped by a short-lived bash one-liner into a user-writable temp/Application Support path, spawned by a non-developer process, is malicious; a uv/rye-managed cache under ~/.local or ~/.cache is likely benign. 2) Contain: kill the interpreter and parent shell, quarantine the dropper, and isolate the host. 3) Hunt: from the same parent, look for the LaunchAgent persistence, keychain/browser collection, and temp/collected_data.zip, then api.telegram.org C2.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has "cpython-3.10.18" or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("cpython-3.10.18","python-build-standalone")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has "cpython-3.10.18" or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("cpython-3.10.18","python-build-standalone")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Gaslight Telegram Bot API getUpdates C2 polling from non-browser macOS process AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts Gaslight's C2: repeated outbound HTTPS to api.telegram.org (Bot API getUpdates polling loop) from a process that is not a browser or the Telegram desktop app. The polling cadence plus the non-browser initiator separates implant beaconing from ordinary Telegram client traffic. Rationale: Uses the article's exact C2 channel (api.telegram.org Bot API getUpdates polling loop) and the runtime-supplied-token detail; SentinelOne confirms the getUpdates polling loop and self-redacting token constructor. Browser/Telegram-app exclusion plus a polling threshold keeps it implant-specific. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/labs/macos-gaslight-rust-backdoor-turns-prompt-injection-on-the-analyst-not-the-sandbox/ • https://cyberpress.org/gaslight-backdoor-misleads-analysts/

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment

  • CLI Telegram clients (e.g. telegram-cli, tdlib-based tools) not on the exclusion list
  • Developer tooling sending CI notifications via the Bot API
  • A user's third-party Telegram client whose process name differs from the exclusion list

| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "/Applications/"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating binary — an unsigned/ad-hoc Rust binary in a user/temp path beaconing to api.telegram.org on a fixed cadence is the implant; a known notification script is benign. 2) Contain: block api.telegram.org egress for the host, kill the process, and capture the binary for the bot-token (note the implant self-redacts it from its own logs). 3) Hunt: correlate with the com.apple.system.services.activity LaunchAgent, the cpython-3.10.18 stager, and sendDocument/attach:// uploads of temp/collected_data.zip.

Gaslight collection archive temp/collected_data.zip staged for Telegram exfiltration AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the exact staging artifact Gaslight's Python suite produces: a ZIP named collected_data.zip written under a temp/ directory aggregating keychain, browser, shell-history and host-profile loot prior to Telegram upload. The hardcoded relative path temp/collected_data.zip is a high-fidelity, campaign-specific indicator. Rationale: Uses the article's literal staging path 'temp/collected_data.zip' — a unique, non-generic filename quoted directly by SentinelOne — making this a low-FP, campaign-specific collection indicator. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/labs/macos-gaslight-rust-backdoor-turns-prompt-injection-on-the-analyst-not-the-sandbox/ • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/macos-gaslight-rust-backdoor/

Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment

  • Security analyst re-running the sample in a sandbox
  • Data-export tooling using a generic 'collected_data' naming convention
  • Backup software temporarily naming an archive collected_data.zip
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the writing process and contents — a ZIP authored by the cpython-3.10.18 collector containing login.keychain-db plus browser profile files is confirmed loot. 2) Contain: isolate the host before upload completes, preserve the ZIP for IR, kill the collector and parent implant, and force-reset credentials for any browser/keychain accounts on that host. 3) Hunt: look for subsequent api.telegram.org sendDocument/attach:// uploads, the LaunchAgent persistence, and the same actor hash elsewhere in the estate.

| order by Timestamp desc

| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSize, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Gaslight credential theft: macOS keychain + Chrome/Brave/Firefox/Safari store access AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts Gaslight's credential-access stage: a non-system process (the staged Python collector or shell) reading the macOS login keychain and browser credential stores — login.keychain-db, Chrome/Brave 'Login Data', Firefox key4.db/logins.json. Catches the loot-harvest step before it is zipped and uploaded. Rationale: Targets the exact credential stores named in the article (macOS Keychain plus Chrome/Brave/Firefox/Safari), with the cpython-3.10.18 collector as the high-fidelity parent pivot; SentinelOne confirms the Python module copies the login keychain database and browser data. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/labs/macos-gaslight-rust-backdoor-turns-prompt-injection-on-the-analyst-not-the-sandbox/ • https://thearabianpost.com/gaslight-malware-exposes-ai-triage-blind-spot/
ATT&CKT1555.001 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A user running `security dump-keychain` or browser-password export tooling legitimately
  • Password managers / migration utilities reading key4.db, logins.json or Login Data
  • Admin troubleshooting keychain corruption from the shell
  • Backup tools that copy browser profile directories (note: direct file reads by the implant may not surface in cmdline telemetry, so pair with the cpython-3.10.18 parent)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("1Password","keychain-access","BitwardenAutoFill")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating process — credential-store access by a cpython-3.10.18 interpreter or an ad-hoc shell descended from the implant is malicious; an interactive admin or known password manager is benign. 2) Contain: isolate the host and treat all credentials stored in that keychain and the four browsers as compromised — rotate passwords, session tokens and SSH/cloud keys. 3) Hunt: confirm the chain by locating temp/collected_data.zip and api.telegram.org uploads, then the com.apple.system.services.activity LaunchAgent for persistence.

ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("6328567511d88fdc2ae0939c5ef17b7a63d2a833881900de018a4f12f4982525", "77b4fd46994992f0e57302cfe76ed23c0d90101381d2b89fc2ddf5c4536e77ca", "baabf249c77bc54c54ab0e66e15af798bd28aa5b4683554456a8b73ab8741239", "b3c56d689414343589f38394d19ba2fe9a518133281200faa0556ba4e4136394") or SHA1 in~ ("6328567511d88fdc2ae0939c5ef17b7a63d2a833881900de018a4f12f4982525", "77b4fd46994992f0e57302cfe76ed23c0d90101381d2b89fc2ddf5c4536e77ca", "baabf249c77bc54c54ab0e66e15af798bd28aa5b4683554456a8b73ab8741239", "b3c56d689414343589f38394d19ba2fe9a518133281200faa0556ba4e4136394") or MD5 in~ ("6328567511d88fdc2ae0939c5ef17b7a63d2a833881900de018a4f12f4982525", "77b4fd46994992f0e57302cfe76ed23c0d90101381d2b89fc2ddf5c4536e77ca", "baabf249c77bc54c54ab0e66e15af798bd28aa5b4683554456a8b73ab8741239", "b3c56d689414343589f38394d19ba2fe9a518133281200faa0556ba4e4136394")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("6328567511d88fdc2ae0939c5ef17b7a63d2a833881900de018a4f12f4982525", "77b4fd46994992f0e57302cfe76ed23c0d90101381d2b89fc2ddf5c4536e77ca", "baabf249c77bc54c54ab0e66e15af798bd28aa5b4683554456a8b73ab8741239", "b3c56d689414343589f38394d19ba2fe9a518133281200faa0556ba4e4136394") or SHA1 in~ ("6328567511d88fdc2ae0939c5ef17b7a63d2a833881900de018a4f12f4982525", "77b4fd46994992f0e57302cfe76ed23c0d90101381d2b89fc2ddf5c4536e77ca", "baabf249c77bc54c54ab0e66e15af798bd28aa5b4683554456a8b73ab8741239", "b3c56d689414343589f38394d19ba2fe9a518133281200faa0556ba4e4136394") or MD5 in~ ("6328567511d88fdc2ae0939c5ef17b7a63d2a833881900de018a4f12f4982525", "77b4fd46994992f0e57302cfe76ed23c0d90101381d2b89fc2ddf5c4536e77ca", "baabf249c77bc54c54ab0e66e15af798bd28aa5b4683554456a8b73ab8741239", "b3c56d689414343589f38394d19ba2fe9a518133281200faa0556ba4e4136394")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["6328567511d88fdc2ae0939c5ef17b7a63d2a833881900de018a4f12f4982525", "77b4fd46994992f0e57302cfe76ed23c0d90101381d2b89fc2ddf5c4536e77ca", "baabf249c77bc54c54ab0e66e15af798bd28aa5b4683554456a8b73ab8741239", "b3c56d689414343589f38394d19ba2fe9a518133281200faa0556ba4e4136394"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Delivery. Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Article-specific behavioural hunt — New Mistic Backdoor Linked to KongTuke in ClickFix and ModeloRAT Campaigns
Installation. Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Mistic / ModeloRAT C2 beacon to KongTuke domains and IPs · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
Mistic backdoor DLL side-load: MpExtMs.exe loading rogue version.dll / EndpointDlp.dll AIInstallation High
Hunts the Mistic (MLTBackdoor) side-loading chain where the legitimate Microsoft Defender binary MpExtMs.exe loads a malicious version.dll loader and EndpointDlp.dll payload from a non-Defender directory. Targets the specific signed-binary-masquerade Symantec documented, not generic DLL side-loading. Rationale: Symantec named the exact triad: legitimate MpExtMs.exe sideloading version.dll (loader hooking GetModuleFileNameW/LoadLibraryW) and EndpointDlp.dll (Mistic payload). Legit loads of these DLLs come from System32/Defender dirs, so a non-standard load path is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.security.com/blog-post/new-mistic-backdoor-modelorat • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/stealthy-mistic-backdoor-linked-to-ransomware-access-broker-kongtuke/
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security testers/red teams copying Defender binaries to a sandbox for analysis
  • Legacy software bundling its own version.dll alongside a copied MS binary in Program Files
  • Defender platform upgrade staging in a temporary ProgramData subfolder not yet matched by the exclusion list
  • EDR/AV self-protection unpacking signed MS binaries to a temp directory
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files\Windows Defender\" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Windows Defender\Platform\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: Pull the full image-load and process tree for the offending MpExtMs.exe instance; confirm the parent and the SHA256 of version.dll/EndpointDlp.dll against the Symantec hash set and VirusTotal. 2) Contain: Network-isolate the host and quarantine the dropped DLLs and the relocated MpExtMs.exe folder; the backdoor runs in-memory so capture a memory image before reboot. 3) Hunt: Sweep the estate for the same DLL filenames outside Defender paths and for outbound connections to the Mistic C2 domains/IPs; check for ModeloRAT/Qilin follow-on tooling.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "MpExtMs.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("version.dll","EndpointDlp.dll")
| where not(FolderPath has @"\Windows Defender\" or FolderPath has @"\Windows\System32\" or FolderPath has @"\WinSxS\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessSHA256, LoadedDll = FileName, LoadedDllPath = FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
// Sentinel lacks a clean image-load table; pivot on MpExtMs.exe executing outside the Defender install paths (the side-load drop site)
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\MpExtMs.exe"
| where not(NewProcessName has "\\Windows Defender\\" or NewProcessName has "\\System32\\")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
title: Mistic Backdoor DLL Side-Load via MpExtMs.exe
id: 7c2f4a1e-9b3d-4e6a-8c1f-2a5d7e9c4b30
description: MpExtMs.exe (Microsoft Defender) loading version.dll or EndpointDlp.dll from a non-Defender, non-System32 directory - Backdoor.Mistic side-load chain
references:
  - https://www.security.com/blog-post/new-mistic-backdoor-modelorat
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/new-mistic-backdoor-linked-to-kongtuke.html

detection:

    Image|endswith: '\MpExtMs.exe'
    ImageLoaded|endswith:
      - '\version.dll'
      - '\EndpointDlp.dll'
  filter_legit:

      - '\Windows Defender\'
      - '\System32\'
      - '\WinSxS\'
  condition: selection and not filter_legit

source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\\MpExtMs.exe OR *\\mpextms.exe OR *\\MPEXTMS.EXE) -@Image:(*\\Windows Defender\\* OR *\\System32\\* OR *\\WinSxS\\*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\MpExtMs\.exe$/i
| NOT (ImageFileName=/\\Windows Defender\\/i)
| NOT (ImageFileName=/\\System32\\/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, SHA256HashData], function=count())

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

KongTuke ClickFix DNS staging: nslookup TXT queries to Mistic/ModeloRAT domains AIDelivery High
Hunts the ClickFix delivery vector where a victim pastes a Win+R command that runs nslookup against attacker-controlled domains using TXT records as a payload staging/signaling channel. Anchored on the specific KongTuke staging domains plus the nslookup-TXT pattern Microsoft documented. Rationale: Combines the Microsoft-documented nslookup TXT staging pattern with KongTuke's confirmed staging domains (updater-worelos.com, upd-domain-goloro.com, etc.). nslookup querying TXT records for these registrable domains, or launched from explorer.exe (Run dialog), is the exact ClickFix delivery shape. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/02/microsoft-discloses-dns-based-clickfix.html • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/26/c/kongtuke-clickfix-abuse-of-compromised-wordpress-sites.html
ATT&CKT1071.004 T1204.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT admin manually running nslookup -type=txt to debug SPF/DKIM/DMARC records (but not against these specific domains)
  • Email-security tooling validating sender TXT records from explorer-launched scripts
  • Network monitoring scripts enumerating TXT records for asset inventory
  • Penetration test replicating the ClickFix lure in an authorized exercise
Suppression filter
| where AccountName !endswith "$" and ProcessCommandLine !has "_dmarc" and ProcessCommandLine !has "_domainkey"
Response runbook
1) Triage: Capture the full nslookup command line and decode the TXT response if still cached; identify the user and confirm whether a Win+R/clipboard paste preceded it (check recent RunMRU registry and clipboard). 2) Contain: Isolate the host and reset the user's credentials; the staged payload typically pipes into PowerShell and pulls ModeloRAT/Mistic. 3) Hunt: Look for a child PowerShell/ZIP download to azwsappdev[.]com-style infra, the MpExtMs.exe side-load chain, and DNS to the other KongTuke domains across the estate.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "nslookup.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-type=txt","-q=txt","-querytype=txt","type=txt")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("updater-worelos.com","upd-domain-goloro.com","authorized-logins.net","upscale-kolo.com","update-fall.com","sql-updater-service.com","rotoa-upda-lo.com","human-check.top","grande-luna.top")
   or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","cmd.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\nslookup.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("-type=txt","-q=txt","-querytype=txt","type=txt")
| where CommandLine has_any ("updater-worelos.com","upd-domain-goloro.com","authorized-logins.net","upscale-kolo.com","update-fall.com","sql-updater-service.com","rotoa-upda-lo.com","human-check.top","grande-luna.top")
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\\explorer.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "\\cmd.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName

Mistic / ModeloRAT C2 beacon to KongTuke domains and IPs AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on host connections or DNS lookups to the confirmed Mistic/ModeloRAT command-and-control domains and IP addresses. Pure named-IOC network detection for KongTuke infrastructure cross-validated by Symantec. Rationale: All domains and IPs are taken verbatim from the article and confirmed in the Symantec IOC table, so any resolution/connection is a direct KongTuke infrastructure hit. Matching registrable domains via endswith/has_any also catches the documented subdomains (mails., defs., ftps., nano., etc.). Cross-checked against: • https://www.security.com/blog-post/new-mistic-backdoor-modelorat • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/stealthy-mistic-backdoor-linked-to-ransomware-access-broker-kongtuke/
ATT&CKT1071.004 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel platform or sandbox detonating samples and resolving the C2 domains for enrichment
  • Security researcher manually browsing the IOC domains from an analyst workstation
  • Passive DNS / sinkhole infrastructure resolving the domains
  • DigitalOcean-hosted IP (142.93.242.144) reuse for an unrelated legitimate service after takedown
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe") or RemoteIP in ("142.93.242.144","144.31.53.78","198.13.159.44","199.91.221.42")
Response runbook
1) Triage: Identify the initiating process for the connection (DeviceNetworkEvents InitiatingProcessFileName) - confirm whether it is MpExtMs.exe, a python.exe (ModeloRAT), or a browser. 2) Contain: Isolate the host, block the domains/IPs at perimeter and DNS, and capture memory before reboot (Mistic is memory-resident). 3) Hunt: Pivot from the host to the MpExtMs.exe side-load and nslookup ClickFix detections, and check for Qilin ransomware staging or lateral movement from the same asset.

   or RemoteIP in ("142.93.242.144","144.31.53.78","198.13.159.44","199.91.221.42")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
union

Backdoor.Mistic loader/payload file hash sweep AIInstallation Medium
Sweeps process, file, and image-load telemetry for the nine confirmed Backdoor.Mistic SHA256 hashes (backdoor variants, loader, privilege-escalation tool, fake lock screen). Direct known-bad hash detection for the Symantec-published sample set. Rationale: Nine SHA256 hashes published in the Symantec IOC table covering Mistic backdoor variants, the loader, the privilege-escalation tool, and the fake lock screen. Exact-hash matches are zero-FP true-positive signals for these specific samples. Cross-checked against: • https://www.security.com/blog-post/new-mistic-backdoor-modelorat
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1620
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware analyst or sandbox intentionally executing a sample of the same hash for research
  • EDR/AV quarantine re-scan re-touching the file and re-emitting a file event
  • Hash collision is cryptographically implausible for SHA256 so a match is effectively definitive
  • Threat-intel ingestion tooling writing the sample to a malware repository share
Response runbook
1) Triage: Confirm the event is a real execution/write on a production endpoint (not a sandbox/analyst host) and capture the parent process and folder path. 2) Contain: Isolate the host, quarantine the file, and capture memory before reboot since Mistic executes in-memory and can self-delete. 3) Hunt: Pivot to the MpExtMs.exe side-load, ClickFix nslookup, and C2 detections on the same host; sweep the estate for the remaining eight hashes and any KongTuke domain resolutions.
let MisticHashes = dynamic(["1e41c7bfaa6aa3b93b6cc024274a10e33f3e12fe7c98c1db387ef8927f9d1984","34d798a6c55e57ed0932b6499f4fbcb5454bdfca903307be101a0594b0ac07bc","3f797a639bc855bc6d5471f327924b62d10900ddec49b970eca6604142bbb4be","59e3c4cb06331b4f2d78a9a0592f3747e573bd01c5a7650c26361d1e25520712","8c935feec4bd05d5d918df308be417532fb42608fb989a08eab183e0ae699235","afd5f1ed45a9867daf3bc64152cef460a06b164c8183e490db39146d4749a82c","db972979d508e75fe730d3b72c2701470fbdaeaf8ebdd674744754fa44438ca5","f591275a8f014b29e567529d67c54eb7bb4473db1c38737d6bfd5b3d52c9344e","fb3630822b70bacb56aa4cec29b5a0e3e9acb3920809e70310a4003385a6d34a"]);
union
(DeviceProcessEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where SHA256 in (MisticHashes) | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Source="Process", FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName),
(DeviceFileEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where SHA256 in (MisticHashes) | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Source="File", FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName),

| order by Timestamp desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")

          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Mass npm Supply Chain Attack: 20 Leo Platform Packages Compromised

StepSecurity
2026-06-25 7 use cases 3 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

On June 24, 2026, an attacker published malicious versions of 20 npm packages belonging to the Leo Platform ecosystem in a coordinated burst spanning less than three seconds. All 20 packages carry an identical CI/CD attack toolkit that steals secrets from GitHub Actions runners, cloud credential stores, package registries, and password managers, then exfiltrates them via the victim's own GitHub token. Together these packages receive approximately 13,600 downloads per week.

Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] GitHub Actions Runner.Worker memory read via /proc/<pid>/mem (CI secret unmasking)
Bun v1.3.13 runtime pulled from GitHub Releases during npm install (Phantom Gyp staging) AICommand & Control High
Hunts the Leo Platform / Miasma toolkit fetching the pinned Bun v1.3.13 single-file binary from github.com/oven-sh/bun/releases during a node/npm install. The stealer runs its core logic under this downloaded Bun runtime specifically to evade Node-child monitoring, so an install-context process reaching this exact release URL is a high-fidelity stager signal. Rationale: Anchored on the article's exact version-pinned Bun download URL (github.com/oven-sh/bun/releases/download/bun-v1.3.13/) scoped to install-tooling initiators; Snyk and Microsoft both confirm the downloaded-Bun evasion for the same toolkit. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/binding-gyp-npm-supply-chain-attack-spreads-like-worm • https://snyk.io/blog/bun-based-stealer-hits-sap-cap-js-mbt-npm-packages/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/05/20/mini-shai-hulud-compromised-antv-npm-packages-enable-ci-cd-credential-theft/
ATT&CKT1105 T1195.002
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate projects that genuinely vendor Bun v1.3.13 and download it during CI build (e.g. Bun-based test suites)
  • Internal mirror/proxy caching the Bun release that then serves it to many build agents
  • Developer manually pinning bun-v1.3.13 in a setup script invoked by npm postinstall of a trusted package
  • Renovate/Dependabot dry-run installs that fetch toolchains
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("bun-types","@biomejs") and DeviceName startswith "trusted-bun-ci")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the package + version being installed when the download fired (correlate InitiatingProcessCommandLine / build log) and confirm whether the repo legitimately uses Bun; check the host against the 20 Leo Platform packages and the 2026-06-24T23:04:55Z publish window. 2) Contain: isolate/cordon the runner, revoke the GITHUB_TOKEN and any cloud creds (AWS/GCP/Azure/Vault) reachable from it, and rotate npm publish tokens for accounts that ran the build. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host/account for bun executing /tmp/p*.js, /proc/<pid>/mem reads of Runner.Worker, and sudoers NOPASSWD writes; search the org for any leo-* package at the malicious versions in package-lock files.
DeviceNetworkEvents

| where RemoteUrl has_any ("oven-sh/bun/releases/download/bun-v1.3.13", "bun-v1.3.13")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","npm","node-gyp","bun","yarn","pnpm")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc

GitHub Actions Runner.Worker memory read via /proc/<pid>/mem (CI secret unmasking) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the toolkit locating the GitHub Actions Runner.Worker process and reading /proc/<pid>/mem directly (sometimes via a sudo python3 helper) to recover secrets that are masked in workflow logs. Reading another process's /proc memory on a CI runner is definitively malicious and is the campaign's core credential-access step. Rationale: Uses the article's definitive CI indicator (read of /proc/{pid}/mem where the target is Runner.Worker); the regex on /proc/<pid>/mem captures both the direct-read and sudo-python3 helper variants documented by Microsoft for the same toolkit. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/binding-gyp-npm-supply-chain-attack-spreads-like-worm • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/05/20/mini-shai-hulud-compromised-antv-npm-packages-enable-ci-cd-credential-theft/
ATT&CKT1003.007 T1212
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate debuggers/profilers (gdb, perf, gcore) attaching to a process during a build-time crash dump
  • Container/runtime health tooling snapshotting memory for diagnostics
  • Security agents themselves enumerating /proc (allowlist the EDR/AV process)
  • Coredump collection scripts that copy /proc/<pid>/mem ranges
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("gdb","gcore","perf","mdatp","wdavdaemon","crash")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the reader is NOT a known debugger/EDR and that the target PID resolves to Runner.Worker (check /proc/<pid>/cmdline access just before); treat any read in a GitHub Actions context as confirmed. 2) Contain: kill the runner, revoke the workflow GITHUB_TOKEN/OIDC token immediately and rotate every secret exposed to that workflow (cloud keys, registry tokens, 1Password items). 3) Hunt: look for the preceding Bun v1.3.13 download and subsequent GitHub GraphQL writes to newly-created dead-drop repos under the build's own token, and check for npm bypass_2fa republish activity.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"/proc/[0-9]+/mem"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage matches regex @"/proc/[0-9]+/mem"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Facility, ProcessName, ProcessID, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Passwordless sudo backdoor written for runner account (runner ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL) AIInstallation High
Hunts the toolkit granting itself passwordless sudo on GitHub-hosted runners by writing 'runner ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL' into the sudoers configuration. The exact account+NOPASSWD string is a narrow, high-fidelity privilege-escalation indicator unique to this campaign's runner targeting. Rationale: Anchored on the article's verbatim escalation string 'runner ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL'; matching NOPASSWD:ALL plus the runner principal keeps it tight to this campaign's GitHub-hosted-runner targeting rather than generic sudoers edits. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/mass-npm-supply-chain-attack-20-leo-platform-packages-compromised • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/binding-gyp-npm-supply-chain-attack-spreads-like-worm
ATT&CKT1548.003 T1098
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Provisioning/IaC (Ansible, cloud-init) that legitimately grants the runner/build user NOPASSWD sudo on self-hosted runners
  • Container base-image build steps adding a NOPASSWD entry for a service account named runner
  • Admins troubleshooting sudo on a CI host
  • Vendor runner setup scripts that intentionally configure passwordless sudo
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("ansible","cloud-init","python3-ansible","chef-client","puppet")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the sudoers write originated from a known provisioning tool/parent (Ansible, cloud-init) or from a build/npm-install descendant; the latter is malicious. 2) Contain: remove the sudoers entry, terminate the runner, and rotate credentials reachable from it; for ephemeral GitHub-hosted runners assume the runner is fully compromised and tear it down. 3) Hunt: correlate with the same host's Bun v1.3.13 download, /proc/<pid>/mem reads, and any GitHub Actions workflow files modified to add id-token: write and attacker-pinned action SHAs.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine contains "NOPASSWD:ALL" and ProcessCommandLine has "runner"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessCommandLine contains "NOPASSWD:ALL" and TargetProcessCommandLine has "runner"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Bun executes dropped temp payload /tmp/p*.js (Miasma stealer launch) AIExploitation High
Hunts the downloaded Bun runtime executing the toolkit's dropped payload at /tmp/p*.js — the definitive behavioral indicator that the obfuscated stealer logic has launched out-of-band from the Node install process. Bun running a script out of /tmp during a package install is anomalous and campaign-specific. Rationale: Uses the article's stated payload drop/exec location (/tmp/p*.js executed by bun) tied to the bun binary name; this parent-runtime + temp-path JS combination is the campaign's definitive behavioral execution indicator and near-zero in normal builds. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/mass-npm-supply-chain-attack-20-leo-platform-packages-compromised • https://snyk.io/blog/bun-based-stealer-hits-sap-cap-js-mbt-npm-packages/
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer running an ad-hoc Bun script saved under /tmp during local debugging
  • CI scratch scripts written to /tmp and executed by a Bun-based build that happen to match the p*.js pattern
  • Test harnesses that generate temp .js fixtures and run them under Bun
  • Bun's own cache/transpile artifacts if relocated to /tmp
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","npm","node-gyp","sh","bash","yarn","pnpm")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the /tmp/p*.js contents (or its hash) before it self-deletes and confirm the parent chain is node/npm install rather than an intentional Bun project. 2) Contain: kill the bun process and runner, revoke the workflow token and rotate all cloud/registry/Vault/1Password secrets exposed to the job. 3) Hunt: pivot to the host's outbound Bun v1.3.13 download, /proc/<pid>/mem Runner.Worker reads, sudoers NOPASSWD writes, and any npm publishes via bypass_2fa from accounts that ran the build; scan repos for leo-* packages pinned to the malicious versions.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "bun"
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"/tmp/p[^/ ]*\.js"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetProcessName has "bun"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine matches regex @"/tmp/p[^/ ]*\.js"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.

      AND (Filesystem.file_path="*/dev/null*" OR Filesystem.file_name IN ("index.js"))
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, Filesystem.process_name,
       Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.file_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
]
High

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Gamaredon HTA downloader auto-executing from Startup folder at logon (mshta.exe) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Gamaredon WinRAR CVE-2025-8088 ADS path-traversal dropping HTA/VBS into Startup folder · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Gamaredon dead-drop C&C resolution via Telegra.ph and GoFile from script hosts · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Gamaredon stealer exfiltration to S3-compatible cloud storage (Wasabi/Tebi/Intercolo) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Gamaredon WinRAR CVE-2025-8088 ADS path-traversal dropping HTA/VBS into Startup folder AIInstallation High
Hunts the persistence step Gamaredon adopted from 2025-09-26: a malicious RAR archive exploiting WinRAR CVE-2025-8088 (alternate-data-stream path traversal) to write an HTA/VBS/VBE/LNK downloader into the user's Startup folder so it auto-runs at next login. Article-specific because it pins the writing process to WinRAR-family binaries and the target to the Startup directory. Rationale: Uses the article's concrete persistence pivot (CVE-2025-8088 → HTA/VBS into Startup folder, active from 2025-09-26) and the WinRAR extraction binaries; Mandiant/Google and SOC Prime confirm the same ADS-to-Startup write pattern (.hta/.vbs/.vbe) across multiple Russia-aligned actors, so it is second-sourced. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/exploiting-critical-winrar-vulnerability • https://socprime.com/active-threats/cve-2025-8088-critical-winrar-vulnerability/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/winrar-path-traversal-flaw-still-exploited-by-numerous-hackers/amp/
ATT&CKT1547.001 T1203 T1564.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate installers shipped as RAR self-extractors that legitimately add a startup launcher
  • IT-deployed login scripts (.vbs/.lnk) packaged in archives by an admin
  • Software that bundles an updater shortcut into Startup after archive extraction
  • Security/portable apps extracted with WinRAR that create a startup auto-run by design
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("/sfx","setup","install") and InitiatingProcessAccountName endswith "$")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the dropped file's full path/hash and the parent RAR archive; detonate or read the HTA/VBS content for a download URL and confirm WinRAR version < 7.13 on the host. 2) Contain: delete/quarantine the Startup-folder artifact, isolate the host before next logon (the payload fires at login), and block any URLs/domains found in the script. 3) Hunt: search the org for the same archive SHA256 in mail/download telemetry, for other hosts running unpatched WinRAR, and for follow-on mshta/wscript execution and connections to telegra.ph / gofile.io / S3 storage domains.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has @"\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\"
| where FileName endswith ".hta" or FileName endswith ".vbs" or FileName endswith ".vbe" or FileName endswith ".lnk"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("winrar.exe","rar.exe","unrar.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("winrar.exe","rar.exe","unrar.exe")
| where TargetFilePath has @"\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\"
| where TargetFileExtension in~ ("hta","vbs","vbe","lnk")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: WinRAR CVE-2025-8088 Script Drop into Startup Folder
id: a3f8c1d2-4b6e-4f21-9c7a-1e2d3f4a5b6c
description: Detects WinRAR-family process writing an HTA/VBS/VBE/LNK file into the user Startup folder, consistent with CVE-2025-8088 path-traversal persistence used by Gamaredon in 2025.
references:

author: SOC Detection Engineering

logsource:

detection:

level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @Image:(*\WinRAR.exe OR *\winrar.exe OR *\Rar.exe OR *\rar.exe OR *\UnRAR.exe OR *\unrar.exe) @TargetFilename:(*\Startup\*.hta OR *\Startup\*.vbs OR *\Startup\*.vbe OR *\Startup\*.lnk)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| ContextImageFileName=/\\(winrar|rar|unrar)\.exe$/i

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_path="*\\Start Menu\\Programs\\Startup\\*") AND (Filesystem.file_name="*.hta" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.vbs" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.vbe" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.lnk") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | search process_name IN ("winrar.exe","rar.exe","unrar.exe") | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Gamaredon HTA downloader auto-executing from Startup folder at logon (mshta.exe) AIExploitation High
Hunts execution of the persisted Gamaredon HTA downloader: mshta.exe launched at user logon with a command line referencing an .hta inside the Startup folder. Complements the file-write detection by catching execution even when the original drop was missed. Rationale: Pins to the article's specific persistence-to-execution chain (HTA downloader placed in Startup executes at next login) and the LOLBin mshta with a Startup-path command line, a combination with near-zero legitimate occurrence; corroborated by Google/Mandiant noting HTA-in-Startup as the second-stage downloader. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/exploiting-critical-winrar-vulnerability
ATT&CKT1218.005 T1547.001 T1059.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legacy in-house HTA-based dashboard intentionally placed in Startup by IT
  • Vendor application that uses an HTA splash/launcher auto-started at logon
  • Admin troubleshooting that temporarily drops an HTA in Startup
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the mshta command line and the referenced .hta path; read the HTA body for embedded URLs/next-stage (PteroSand VBScript) and check whether a RAR/CVE-2025-8088 drop preceded it. 2) Contain: kill the mshta process, remove the Startup artifact, isolate the host, and block extracted C2/dead-drop domains. 3) Hunt: pivot on the user/host for child wscript/cscript execution, temporary .vbs written-then-deleted (PteroDum), and egress to telegra.ph, gofile.io, or S3 storage providers.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "mshta.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has @"\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\"
| where ProcessCommandLine has ".hta"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName has "mshta.exe"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has @"\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has ".hta"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Gamaredon stealer exfiltration to S3-compatible cloud storage (Wasabi/Tebi/Intercolo) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts PteroVDoor/PteroPSDoor's 2025 primary exfiltration channel: scripted upload of stolen files to S3-compatible storage at wasabisys.com, tebi.io, or i3storage.com (Intercolo de-fra.i3storage.com) initiated by a script host rather than a browser. High-fidelity because exfil from wscript/powershell/mshta to these specific providers is anomalous. Rationale: Uses the corroborated exfil endpoints (Wasabi=wasabisys.com, Tebi=tebi.io, Intercolo=de-fra.i3storage.com) named as Gamaredon's 2025 primary exfil channel, scoped to script-host initiators to suppress normal browser/backup S3 traffic; ESET's own write-up and the search-confirmed config-rotation (Wasabi→Tebi→Intercolo) second-source the domains. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/gamaredon-2025-leveraging-tunnels-workers-dead-drops-new-alliances/ • https://www.govinfosecurity.com/russias-gamaredon-adapts-tactics-to-target-ukraine-a-32068
ATT&CKT1567.002 T1059.001 T1059.005
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Corporate backup/sync software legitimately using Wasabi S3 (but normally via its own binary, not wscript/powershell)
  • Developer/DevOps PowerShell scripts pushing artifacts to a sanctioned Wasabi/Tebi bucket
  • A red-team or admin ad-hoc PowerShell aws/s3 upload
  • Telemetry where a browser helper is misattributed as the initiating process
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("aws s3","Backup","veeam") and InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ ("backupsvc","svc-backup"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating script host, its command line, and the volume/bytes uploaded; confirm the bucket/host is not a sanctioned corporate storage account. 2) Contain: block the storage FQDNs at the proxy/firewall, isolate the host, and preserve the stealer binary/script for analysis. 3) Hunt: trace back to the persistence/execution chain (mshta-from-Startup, WinRAR drop), enumerate which files were staged/read prior to upload, and sweep other hosts for DNS to the same three providers.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("wasabisys.com","tebi.io","i3storage.com")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","cmd.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has_any ("wasabisys.com","tebi.io","i3storage.com")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Gamaredon dead-drop C&C resolution via Telegra.ph and GoFile from script hosts AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts PteroOdd (Telegra.ph API) and PteroEffigy (GoFile) fetching next-stage payloads / resolving C&C from legitimate dead-drop services, requested by a Windows script host. Article-specific because it targets the exact two services named for these downloaders rather than generic LOLBin egress. Rationale: Targets the two specific dead-drop services the article ties to named downloaders (PteroOdd→Telegra.ph API, PteroEffigy→GoFile) and scopes to script-host initiators so normal browser visits to telegra.ph/gofile are excluded; flagged Medium because only the original ESET piece names these two services for these tools. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/gamaredon-2025-leveraging-tunnels-workers-dead-drops-new-alliances/
ATT&CKT1102.001 T1105 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A user legitimately downloading a shared file from gofile.io that an EDR attributes to a script wrapper
  • Automation/scripts that scrape telegra.ph articles for benign content
  • Browser child processes mis-tagged as the initiating process
  • Security tooling sandboxing a URL that resolves these domains
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files"
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the script-host command line and the full URL/telegra.ph path or gofile content ID; pull what was downloaded and decode any retrieved next-stage C&C address. 2) Contain: block telegra.ph/gofile.io egress from the host, isolate it, and add the resolved real C&C to blocklists. 3) Hunt: correlate with preceding HTA/mshta execution and following uploads to wasabisys.com/tebi.io/i3storage.com on the same host, and sweep the org for other script hosts touching these dead-drop services.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("telegra.ph","gofile.io")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","cmd.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has_any ("telegra.ph","gofile.io")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'

    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'

            - '\chrome.exe'

    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
