Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Zero-Day CVE-2026-20245 Exploited to Gain Root Access

The Hacker News
2026-06-25 8 use cases 2 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

An unknown threat actor exploited a recently disclosed high-severity security flaw impacting Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN as a zero-day at least two months before it was publicly disclosed, according to new findings from Google-owned Mandiant. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-20245 (CVSS score: 7.8), allows an authenticated, local attacker to execute arbitrary commands with elevated privileges

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Rogue SD-WAN control-plane peering from previously-unseen system-IP (auth-bypass / stolen cert)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Cisco SD-WAN Manager privilege escalation via malicious evil_tenant.csv upload (CVE-2026-20245) · [LLM] su elevation from admin into rogue 'troot' account on Cisco SD-WAN appliance
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Rogue 'troot' root account written to /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow on Cisco SD-WAN Manager · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Zero-Day CVE-2026-20245 Exploited to Gain Root Access
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Anti-forensic admin password change-and-revert on Cisco SD-WAN Manager · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Cisco SD-WAN Manager privilege escalation via malicious evil_tenant.csv upload (CVE-2026-20245) AIExploitation High
Hunts the CVE-2026-20245 exploit primitive: upload/processing of a crafted tenant CSV named evil_tenant.csv on a Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Manager/Controller/Validator that escalates a netadmin account to root. The filename is a confirmed Mandiant IOC and is deleted post-exploit, so the file-create/import event is the catch window. Rationale: evil_tenant.csv is a unique Mandiant-confirmed exploit-file IOC for CVE-2026-20245 with no benign use; a file-import event bearing that exact name on an SD-WAN appliance is near-zero FP. Cross-checked against Google Cloud/Mandiant blog and Cisco PSIRT advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/zero-day-exploitation-cisco-catalyst-sd-wan-manager • https://sec.cloudapps.cisco.com/security/center/content/CiscoSecurityAdvisory/cisco-sa-sdwan-privesc-4uxFrdzx • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/mandiant-reveals-how-cisco-sd-wan-zero-day-attacks-gained-root-access/
ATT&CKT1068
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate tenant onboarding CSV coincidentally named evil_tenant.csv (extremely unlikely in production)
  • A red-team/pentest engagement replaying the public CVE-2026-20245 PoC
  • Forensic IR staging where an analyst copies the recovered exploit sample back onto a lab appliance
  • Backup/restore of a previously compromised config that still references the filename
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the source host is an SD-WAN Manager/Controller/Validator and pull surrounding syslog for the netadmin account that performed the tenant import; check appliance software version against fixed releases (20.9.9.2/20.12.7.2/20.15.4.5/20.15.5.3/20.18.3.1/26.1.1.2). 2) Contain: isolate the appliance from the control plane, force-rotate all admin/netadmin credentials and revoke device certificates, and preserve /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow and config archives before the actor's cleanup script runs. 3) Hunt: search same host for a 'troot' account, su sessions into it, and admin password change-then-revert; check whether a config change was pushed to edge devices.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage has "evil_tenant.csv"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, Facility, ProcessName, SeverityLevel, SyslogMessage
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Rogue 'troot' root account written to /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow on Cisco SD-WAN Manager AIInstallation High
Hunts the persistence step of the CVE-2026-20245 intrusion: creation of a hidden account named 'troot' with UID 0 / root shell in /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow on a Cisco SD-WAN appliance. The username is a confirmed Mandiant IOC and appliances have no native local-account workflow, so any 'troot' creation is high fidelity. Rationale: 'troot' is a Mandiant/GTIG-confirmed rogue UID-0 account name written to /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow; SD-WAN appliances expose no legitimate Linux useradd workflow, so a 'troot' creation token-matched with passwd/shadow context is high-fidelity persistence. Confirmed via Google Cloud blog and BleepingComputer. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/zero-day-exploitation-cisco-catalyst-sd-wan-manager • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/mandiant-reveals-how-cisco-sd-wan-zero-day-attacks-gained-root-access/
ATT&CKT1136.001
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A sysadmin manually creating a local troubleshooting account that happens to contain the string 'troot'
  • Vendor TAC support session creating a temporary diagnostic account
  • Configuration management tooling provisioning local accounts during appliance rebuild
  • Lab/PoC reproduction of the Mandiant intrusion
Response runbook
1) Triage: dump the current /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow, confirm a 'troot' entry exists with UID 0 or a login shell, and identify which admin/netadmin session created it and from what source IP. 2) Contain: disable and delete the troot account, kill any active troot sessions, rotate all appliance credentials and revoke device certs, and snapshot disk before the actor's validation/cleanup script removes the entry. 3) Hunt: pivot to su sessions into troot, the evil_tenant.csv import that preceded it, and admin-password change-and-revert anti-forensics; check sibling appliances in the fabric for the same account.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage has "troot"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("useradd", "/etc/passwd", "/etc/shadow", "new user", "new group", "add-shell")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, ProcessName, Facility, SeverityLevel, SyslogMessage
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

su elevation from admin into rogue 'troot' account on Cisco SD-WAN appliance AIExploitation High
Hunts the corroborated step where the actor, after creating 'troot', authenticated into it via su from the admin context to obtain a full root shell. PAM/auth syslog records 'session opened for user troot', which is independent telemetry from the file-write detection and fires even if file events aren't captured. Rationale: Mandiant confirmed the admin account used su to access the newly created troot account; PAM 'session opened for user troot' is a unique, deterministic string tied to the named rogue account, making it a clean alert distinct from the file-write detection. Verified against Google Cloud/Mandiant reporting. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/zero-day-exploitation-cisco-catalyst-sd-wan-manager • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/mandiant-reveals-how-cisco-sd-wan-zero-day-attacks-gained-root-access/
ATT&CKT1078.003
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate operator who manually created an account literally named troot then su'd into it
  • Lab/PoC reproduction of the intrusion
  • Backup restoration replaying historical auth logs containing the entry
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the originating account (expected: admin) and source IP of the su, and correlate the session timestamp with the troot account creation and the evil_tenant.csv import. 2) Contain: terminate the troot session, delete the account, isolate the appliance from the SD-WAN control plane, and rotate/revoke admin credentials and certificates. 3) Hunt: review all commands executed in the troot root shell (config exfil, edge-device config push), check for the actor's cleanup/validation script, and sweep peer appliances for matching su-to-troot events.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ProcessName has "su" or SyslogMessage has "su"
| where SyslogMessage has "session opened for user troot" or SyslogMessage matches regex @"(?i)su(\[\d+\])?:.*troot"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, ProcessName, SeverityLevel, SyslogMessage
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Anti-forensic admin password change-and-revert on Cisco SD-WAN Manager AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the operational-security technique Mandiant attributed to this actor: the default/admin password was changed (to enable exfiltration of the SD-WAN fabric config) and then restored to its original value so a logging-in administrator would notice nothing. Surfaces hosts where the admin account password is modified two or more times in a short window. Rationale: Mandiant/GTIG explicitly described the actor changing the admin password to exfiltrate the fabric config then reverting it; two password modifications to the admin account on one appliance inside a short window is the temporal signature of that round-trip. A single change is routine, so the >=2-in-window threshold is the discriminator. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/zero-day-exploitation-cisco-catalyst-sd-wan-manager • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/mandiant-reveals-how-cisco-sd-wan-zero-day-attacks-gained-root-access/
ATT&CKT1098 T1070
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A sysadmin who fat-fingers a password reset and immediately corrects it
  • Scheduled credential-rotation tooling that updates then reconciles the admin secret
  • Break-glass procedure that sets and then resets the admin password
  • Vendor TAC session temporarily changing then restoring admin credentials
Suppression filter
// scope to the SD-WAN appliances and drop known rotation tooling identities once enumerated, e.g.:
// | where SyslogMessage !has "cron" and SyslogMessage !has "ansible"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the two+ admin password-change events, confirm whether the final value matches the original (revert), and identify the source IP/session performing them. 2) Contain: force an out-of-band admin password reset and certificate revocation, and review for a fabric-config export occurring between the two changes. 3) Hunt: correlate with troot account creation, su-to-troot sessions, evil_tenant.csv import, and any cleanup/validation script execution; verify no config was pushed to edge devices during the window.
let window = 2h;
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("password changed", "password updated", "passwd")
| where SyslogMessage has "admin"
| summarize pwChanges = count(), firstChange = min(TimeGenerated), lastChange = max(TimeGenerated), Samples = make_list(SyslogMessage, 5) by Computer, bin(TimeGenerated, window)
| where pwChanges >= 2   // change + revert within the same 2h bucket = anti-forensic round-trip
| sort by lastChange desc
source:linux.syslog admin ("password changed" OR "password updated" OR passwd)
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Change.All_Changes where All_Changes.object_category=user All_Changes.action=modified All_Changes.object="admin" by All_Changes.dest All_Changes.user _time span=2h
| `drop_dm_object_name("All_Changes")`
| stats sum(count) as pwChanges values(user) as actors min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime by dest
| where pwChanges >= 2
| `ctime(firstTime)` | `ctime(lastTime)`
| sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Change.All_Changes where All_Changes.object_category=user All_Changes.action=modified All_Changes.object="admin" by All_Changes.dest All_Changes.user _time span=2h
| `drop_dm_object_name("All_Changes")`
| stats sum(count) as pwChanges values(user) as actors min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime by dest
| where pwChanges >= 2
| `ctime(firstTime)` | `ctime(lastTime)`
| sort - lastTime
Rogue SD-WAN control-plane peering from previously-unseen system-IP (auth-bypass / stolen cert) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the initial-access wave Mandiant tied to CVE-2026-20127/CVE-2026-20182 auth-bypass and stolen device certificates: unauthorized control connections (rogue peering) into the SD-WAN fabric from a controller/edge system-IP never observed in the 30-day baseline. Anti-baseline on the peer system-IP parsed from control-connection syslog. Rationale: Mandiant attributed the first/second intrusion waves to rogue peering connections via CVE-2026-20127/20182 auth-bypass or stolen certificates; a control connection from a system-IP absent from the 30-day fabric baseline is the article-specific signature of an unauthorized peer joining the control plane. Lower confidence as it relies on baseline maturity rather than a fixed IOC. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/zero-day-exploitation-cisco-catalyst-sd-wan-manager • https://sec.cloudapps.cisco.com/security/center/content/CiscoSecurityAdvisory/cisco-sa-sdwan-privesc-4uxFrdzx
ATT&CKT1190 T1078
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate onboarding of a new vEdge/cEdge or controller into the fabric
  • Datacenter migration or controller IP re-addressing
  • DR failover bringing a standby controller online with a new system-IP
  • Lab/staging device briefly joining the production overlay
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the new peer system-IP against the authorized device inventory and certificate serials; if unknown, treat as rogue. 2) Contain: quarantine/deny the peer at the controller, revoke any suspected stolen device certificate, and verify control-plane policy hasn't been altered. 3) Hunt: on devices the rogue peer touched, look for CVE-2026-20245 follow-on (evil_tenant.csv, troot account, su-to-troot, password change-and-revert) and review whether any config was pushed to edge devices.
let lookback = 30d;
let baseline = Syslog
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(lookback) .. ago(1d))
    | where SyslogMessage has "control connection"
    | extend PeerIP = extract(@"system-ip\s+(\d{1,3}(?:\.\d{1,3}){3})", 1, SyslogMessage)
    | where isnotempty(PeerIP)
    | distinct PeerIP;
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where SyslogMessage has "control connection"
| extend PeerIP = extract(@"system-ip\s+(\d{1,3}(?:\.\d{1,3}){3})", 1, SyslogMessage)
| where isnotempty(PeerIP)
| join kind=leftanti baseline on PeerIP
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, PeerIP, SeverityLevel, SyslogMessage
| sort by TimeGenerated desc
source:linux.syslog "control connection" (up OR established OR new)
APPLICATION
index=* (sourcetype="cisco:sdwan" OR sourcetype="cisco:vmanage" OR sourcetype="cisco:vsmart" OR sourcetype="cisco:vbond") "control connection"
| rex field=_raw "system-ip\s+(?<peer_system_ip>\d{1,3}(?:\.\d{1,3}){3})"
| where isnotnull(peer_system_ip)
| stats earliest(_time) as firstTime latest(_time) as lastTime count by host peer_system_ip
| eval ageDays=round((now()-firstTime)/86400,1)
| where ageDays < 1
| `ctime(firstTime)` | `ctime(lastTime)`
| sort - firstTime

id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies

references:

simonecorsi/mawesome GitHub Action has been compromised

StepSecurity
2026-06-25 4 use cases 1 technique 3 kill-chain phases detected

On June 24, 2026, an attacker compromised the simonecorsi/mawesome GitHub repository. They force-pushed malicious commits and repointed several version tags to that commit. As a result, any workflow running against those tags after that time executed the attacker's code inside its GitHub Actions runner.

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Compromised simonecorsi/mawesome GitHub Action payload by known hash · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Runner.Worker process memory scrape via /proc on self-hosted GitHub Actions runner · [LLM] First-seen external egress from GitHub Actions Runner.Worker child process
Compromised simonecorsi/mawesome GitHub Action payload by known hash AIInstallation Medium
Hunts for the specific malicious payload pushed to simonecorsi/mawesome during the June 24 2026 tag-poisoning compromise, matched by SHA256/SHA1 on self-hosted GitHub Actions runners monitored by EDR. Fires on file write or process execution of the imposter-commit artifact inside the runner. Rationale: Pivots on the article's three pre-extracted IOCs (SHA256 9f93d77d... and the two SHA1s) which are the imposter-commit payload; a hash match is near-zero-FP, so this is a clean alerting rule for any self-hosted runner that executed a poisoned mawesome tag. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/github-action-tj-actions-changed-files-supply-chain-attack-cve-2025-30066 • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/detecting-and-mitigating-the-tj-actions-changed-files-supply-chain-attack-cve-2025-30066 • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2025/03/18/supply-chain-compromise-third-party-tj-actionschanged-files-cve-2025-30066-and-reviewdogaction
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher detonating the sample in a sandboxed runner for analysis
  • EDR/AV quarantine copy of the file re-scanned generating a benign file event
  • Threat-intel team staging the IOC file on a host for YARA testing
  • Backup/forensic image mounting that re-reads the captured payload
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe") or FolderPath has_any ("\\Quarantine\\", "/quarantine/"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the host is a self-hosted GitHub Actions runner and pull the workflow run that executed it; identify which mawesome tag/SHA was referenced and the repo. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the runner, rotate ALL secrets exposed to that workflow (GITHUB_TOKEN, cloud OIDC roles, registry creds, signing keys) and pin the action to a trusted commit SHA or remove it. 3) HUNT: Search other runners for the same hashes, review egress from the runner during the run window, and check downstream artifacts/packages built by that pipeline for tampering.

Runner.Worker process memory scrape via /proc on self-hosted GitHub Actions runner AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the core mawesome/tj-actions-style payload behaviour: a child process spawned by the GitHub Actions Runner.Worker reading /proc/<pid>/maps or /proc/<pid>/mem to scrape CI/CD secrets from runner memory. Article-specific because it pivots on Runner.Worker as the parent plus the in-image label 'Runner.Worker Memory Scrape'. Rationale: Corroborated by Sysdig/Wiz analyses of the identical tj-actions payload which 'identifies the Runner.Worker process, opens its memory mappings and regex-searches for secrets'; the Runner.Worker parent + /proc maps/mem access is the high-fidelity credential-access signal the thin article only labels as 'Runner.Worker Memory Scrape'. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/detecting-and-mitigating-the-tj-actions-changed-files-supply-chain-attack-cve-2025-30066 • https://www.wiz.io/blog/github-action-tj-actions-changed-files-supply-chain-attack-cve-2025-30066
ATT&CKT1003.007 T1552
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Runner self-diagnostic or crash-dump tooling (gcore/dd) reading worker memory during a hang
  • Performance profilers (perf, py-spy) attached to a build process inside CI
  • Custom debugging step in a workflow that intentionally inspects /proc for troubleshooting
  • Container runtime health checks reading /proc/<pid>/status (excluded by maps/mem filter)
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("py-spy","perf record","/proc/self/status","/proc/meminfo") )
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the full command line of the child process and the workflow YAML that ran; confirm whether a memory-read step was legitimately authored or injected by a third-party action. 2) CONTAIN: Treat every secret available to that job as compromised — rotate tokens/OIDC roles immediately and isolate the runner from further job dispatch. 3) HUNT: Pivot on the same Runner.Worker parent across all runners for /proc memory reads, base64-encoded stdout, and any outbound POST to gist.githubusercontent.com or unknown hosts in the same run window.

| order by Timestamp desc

title: GitHub Actions Runner.Worker Memory Scrape via Proc Filesystem

status: experimental
description: Detects a process spawned by the GitHub Actions Runner.Worker reading /proc/<pid>/maps or /proc/<pid>/mem to scrape CI/CD secrets, as seen in the simonecorsi/mawesome and tj-actions compromises.

First-seen external egress from GitHub Actions Runner.Worker child process AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts for CI/CD secret exfiltration: an interpreter or download tool spawned by Runner.Worker making an outbound connection to a public destination never seen from that runner population before. Targets the 'Credential Exfil' stage of the mawesome compromise. Rationale: Sysdig/Wiz note exfil variants that POST scraped secrets to gist.githubusercontent.com or attacker hosts; pivoting on a Runner.Worker child interpreter making a first-seen public connection isolates the exfil step. Sentinel/Datadog left blank because their available network tables in this tenant cannot attribute the connection back to the Runner.Worker parent process. File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("9f93d77d32833a515bc406c46da477142bb1ac2babeecb6aa42f98669a6db015", "5792aba0e2180b9b80b77644370a6889d5817456", "bcb6b1d409144318e8fad2171d6fe06d02299d1a") or SHA1 in~ ("9f93d77d32833a515bc406c46da477142bb1ac2babeecb6aa42f98669a6db015", "5792aba0e2180b9b80b77644370a6889d5817456", "bcb6b1d409144318e8fad2171d6fe06d02299d1a") or MD5 in~ ("9f93d77d32833a515bc406c46da477142bb1ac2babeecb6aa42f98669a6db015", "5792aba0e2180b9b80b77644370a6889d5817456", "bcb6b1d409144318e8fad2171d6fe06d02299d1a")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("9f93d77d32833a515bc406c46da477142bb1ac2babeecb6aa42f98669a6db015", "5792aba0e2180b9b80b77644370a6889d5817456", "bcb6b1d409144318e8fad2171d6fe06d02299d1a") or SHA1 in~ ("9f93d77d32833a515bc406c46da477142bb1ac2babeecb6aa42f98669a6db015", "5792aba0e2180b9b80b77644370a6889d5817456", "bcb6b1d409144318e8fad2171d6fe06d02299d1a") or MD5 in~ ("9f93d77d32833a515bc406c46da477142bb1ac2babeecb6aa42f98669a6db015", "5792aba0e2180b9b80b77644370a6889d5817456", "bcb6b1d409144318e8fad2171d6fe06d02299d1a")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["9f93d77d32833a515bc406c46da477142bb1ac2babeecb6aa42f98669a6db015", "5792aba0e2180b9b80b77644370a6889d5817456", "bcb6b1d409144318e8fad2171d6fe06d02299d1a"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

codfish/semantic-release-action GitHub Action has been compromised

StepSecurity
2026-06-25 10 use cases 3 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

On June 24, 2026, an attacker compromised the codfish/semantic-release-action GitHub repository. At 15:39:06 UTC they force-pushed a malicious commit and repointed several version tags to that commit. As a result, any workflow running against those tags after that time executed the attacker's code inside its GitHub Actions runner.

Malicious index.js dropped into codfish/semantic-release-action runner checkout AIDelivery Medium
Detects the compromised composite action being checked out onto a self-hosted GitHub Actions runner: the malicious commit ships a ~512KB index.js into the action's _actions checkout directory, whereas the legitimate action was Docker-based and only ever contained entrypoint.js + Dockerfile. Any index.js inside a codfish/semantic-release-action path (or matching the payload hash) indicates the hijacked tag was pulled. Rationale: Anchored on the article's exact facts: the action was converted Docker→composite and a 512KB index.js was added under the action path (_actions/codfish/semantic-release-action). Legit versions never contained index.js, making path+filename and the payload SHA256 (9f93d77d...) high-fidelity. Corroborated by Aikido's independent write-up. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/supply-chain-compromise-codfish-semantic-release-action • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/compromised-github-action-codfish-steals-secrets • https://github.com/codfish/semantic-release-action/activity
ATT&CKT1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A downstream fork that legitimately re-bundles the action as a Node/Bun composite with its own index.js
  • Security researchers replaying the malicious commit in a sandbox runner for analysis
  • Internal mirror/cache of GitHub Actions that retains the old malicious artifact after remediation
  • An unrelated action in a different org that happens to share the 'semantic-release-action' substring in its name
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("defender", "mssense.exe") and FolderPath !has "\\analysis-sandbox\\"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the FolderPath resolves to a GitHub Actions _actions checkout and the file SHA256 = 9f93d77d...; identify which workflow/repo on this runner referenced codfish/semantic-release-action and which tag (v1.6.1–v2.2.1) it pinned. 2) CONTAIN: Take the self-hosted runner offline, rotate every secret that workflow could touch (GITHUB_TOKEN is auto-expired but rotate any NPM_TOKEN/PAT/cloud OIDC trust), and revoke OIDC sessions. 3) HUNT: Pin the action to the clean v5 SHA across the org, search other runners for the same file/hash, and look for the Bun execution and dead-drop C2 (UCs below) on the same host.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where (FolderPath has "semantic-release-action" and FileName =~ "index.js")
   or SHA256 =~ "9f93d77d32833a515bc406c46da477142bb1ac2babeecb6aa42f98669a6db015"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, FileSize, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where (TargetFilePath has "semantic-release-action" and TargetFileName =~ "index.js")
   or TargetFileSHA256 =~ "9f93d77d32833a515bc406c46da477142bb1ac2babeecb6aa42f98669a6db015"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Bun runtime executing payload index.js from semantic-release-action path AIInstallation High
Detects the malicious composite action's injected step running the payload via `bun run <action_path>/index.js`. The attacker deliberately chose Bun over Node to evade Node's --require security hooks. A Bun process whose command line references both the codfish/semantic-release-action path and index.js is the execution stage of the compromise. Rationale: Uses the article's exact execution string `bun run ${{ github.action_path }}/index.js` — the path token 'semantic-release-action' + 'index.js' + the Bun binary is unique to this compromise (legit action ran node /action/entrypoint.js in Docker). The Bun choice for --require evasion is called out explicitly in the article. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/supply-chain-compromise-codfish-semantic-release-action • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/compromised-github-action-codfish-steals-secrets

GitHub dead-drop C2 — commit-search for RevokeAndItGoesKaboom / TheBeautifulSandsOfTime AICommand & Control Medium
Detects the payload's dead-drop C2: it queries the GitHub commit-search API for messages tagged RevokeAndItGoesKaboom (encrypted operator PAT) and TheBeautifulSandsOfTime (RSA-signed eval command). On a TLS-inspecting proxy these unique markers appear verbatim in the request URL; on raw EDR, surface the Bun process resolving/connecting to api.github.com for the same purpose. Rationale: Uses the article's verbatim dead-drop identifiers (RevokeAndItGoesKaboom, TheBeautifulSandsOfTime) and the exact search endpoint /search/commits?q=RevokeAndItGoesKaboom — proxy-visible markers are near-zero FP. The Defender/Falcon variants degrade gracefully to 'Bun reaching api.github.com' since HTTPS hides the query string. Datadog/Sigma omitted: no native GitHub/proxy source maps cleanly to the URL-marker logic and it is multi-shape across telemetry. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/supply-chain-compromise-codfish-semantic-release-action • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/compromised-github-action-codfish-steals-secrets
ATT&CKT1102.001 T1528
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Bun-based tooling that calls the GitHub API during a release (Defender/Falcon variant only)
  • A developer manually searching GitHub commits containing the string 'RevokeAndItGoesKaboom' while researching this incident
  • Threat-intel platforms or scanners crawling GitHub commit search
  • Proxy logging a researcher's reproduction traffic in a sandbox
Suppression filter
| where SrcHostname !has "sandbox" and UserAgent !has "ThreatIntel"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: For proxy hits, confirm the URL contains the literal dead-drop marker and the source is a CI runner/Bun host — that is a confirmed C2 callback. For EDR-only hits, verify the Bun process correlates with the index.js execution UC on the same host/time. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the runner, block egress, and revoke/rotate every token the runner held; assume the operator already pulled a stolen PAT via the dead drop. 3) HUNT: Search org-wide GitHub audit logs for commits/pushes made by stolen tokens, new commits matching RevokeAndItGoesKaboom: or TheBeautifulSandsOfTime: in your repos, and the same campaign fingerprint in @antv/graphlib, echarts-for-react, and tanstack-react-router dependencies.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "bun"
| where RemoteUrl has "github.com" or RemoteUrl has "githubusercontent.com"
| summarize ConnCount=count(), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), Urls=make_set(RemoteUrl,20) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP
| order by FirstSeen desc
// HTTPS hides the ?q=RevokeAndItGoesKaboom query string at the network layer; this surfaces Bun talking to GitHub for triage. Use ImWebSession/proxy for the verbatim marker.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has_any ("RevokeAndItGoesKaboom","TheBeautifulSandsOfTime","search/commits?q=RevokeAndItGoesKaboom")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, Url, UserAgent=HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DstIpAddr, DstHostname
| order by TimeGenerated desc
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest
| DomainName=/(^|\.)github\.com$/i
| ContextImageFileName=/bun/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, DomainName], function=count())
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.url="*RevokeAndItGoesKaboom*" OR Web.url="*TheBeautifulSandsOfTime*" OR Web.url="*search/commits?q=RevokeAndItGoesKaboom*") by Web.src Web.user Web.dest Web.url Web.http_user_agent | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.url="*RevokeAndItGoesKaboom*" OR Web.url="*TheBeautifulSandsOfTime*" OR Web.url="*search/commits?q=RevokeAndItGoesKaboom*") by Web.src Web.user Web.dest Web.url Web.http_user_agent | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK

    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic

    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`

| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("9f93d77d32833a515bc406c46da477142bb1ac2babeecb6aa42f98669a6db015", "6b9501e1889cc45c91726729610cf69c2442b8c5", "5792aba0e2180b9b80b77644370a6889d5817456", "bcb6b1d409144318e8fad2171d6fe06d02299d1a") or SHA1 in~ ("9f93d77d32833a515bc406c46da477142bb1ac2babeecb6aa42f98669a6db015", "6b9501e1889cc45c91726729610cf69c2442b8c5", "5792aba0e2180b9b80b77644370a6889d5817456", "bcb6b1d409144318e8fad2171d6fe06d02299d1a") or MD5 in~ ("9f93d77d32833a515bc406c46da477142bb1ac2babeecb6aa42f98669a6db015", "6b9501e1889cc45c91726729610cf69c2442b8c5", "5792aba0e2180b9b80b77644370a6889d5817456", "bcb6b1d409144318e8fad2171d6fe06d02299d1a")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("9f93d77d32833a515bc406c46da477142bb1ac2babeecb6aa42f98669a6db015", "6b9501e1889cc45c91726729610cf69c2442b8c5", "5792aba0e2180b9b80b77644370a6889d5817456", "bcb6b1d409144318e8fad2171d6fe06d02299d1a") or SHA1 in~ ("9f93d77d32833a515bc406c46da477142bb1ac2babeecb6aa42f98669a6db015", "6b9501e1889cc45c91726729610cf69c2442b8c5", "5792aba0e2180b9b80b77644370a6889d5817456", "bcb6b1d409144318e8fad2171d6fe06d02299d1a") or MD5 in~ ("9f93d77d32833a515bc406c46da477142bb1ac2babeecb6aa42f98669a6db015", "6b9501e1889cc45c91726729610cf69c2442b8c5", "5792aba0e2180b9b80b77644370a6889d5817456", "bcb6b1d409144318e8fad2171d6fe06d02299d1a")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["9f93d77d32833a515bc406c46da477142bb1ac2babeecb6aa42f98669a6db015", "6b9501e1889cc45c91726729610cf69c2442b8c5", "5792aba0e2180b9b80b77644370a6889d5817456", "bcb6b1d409144318e8fad2171d6fe06d02299d1a"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

—
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Rogue SD-WAN peering / vmanage-admin authentication from unexpected source
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Cisco SD-WAN CVE-2026-20245 exploit via malicious 'evil_tenant.csv' tenant upload · [LLM] Privilege pivot via 'su' to rogue root account troot on SD-WAN device
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Rogue root account 'troot' created on Cisco SD-WAN appliance · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Mandiant reveals how Cisco SD-WAN zero-day attacks gained root access
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Anti-forensic backup of /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow on SD-WAN appliance
Cisco SD-WAN CVE-2026-20245 exploit via malicious 'evil_tenant.csv' tenant upload AIExploitation High
Hunts the named exploit payload used to trigger the Catalyst SD-WAN CLI command-injection flaw (CVE-2026-20245). The tenant-upload feature ingesting a file named evil_tenant.csv is the article's single most specific artefact and indicates active root-level privilege escalation on vManage/vSmart/vBond. Rationale: evil_tenant.csv is a unique, attacker-chosen filename confirmed by Mandiant/Google and The Hacker News; no legitimate SD-WAN tenant import uses this name, making it a near-zero-FP exploit signature. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/zero-day-exploitation-cisco-catalyst-sd-wan-manager • https://sec.cloudapps.cisco.com/security/center/content/CiscoSecurityAdvisory/cisco-sa-sdwan-privesc-4uxFrdzx • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/cisco-catalyst-sd-wan-zero-day-cve-2026.html
ATT&CKT1068 T1059.004
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Penetration test or red-team replaying the published Mandiant IOC for validation
  • Threat-hunt or BAS tooling (e.g. Picus) injecting the named artefact during a controlled exercise
  • A customer-authored tenant CSV that coincidentally reuses the 'evil_tenant' name in a lab
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the source device and the authenticated account (likely vmanage-admin or a recently-restored admin) that invoked the tenant-upload; pull the appliance's full CLI/audit log for that session. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the SD-WAN Manager/Controller from peer and edge connectivity, force-rotate admin and vmanage-admin credentials and certificates, and snapshot the device before remediation. Step 3 (hunt): Search for follow-on 'troot' account creation, su pivots, and /etc/passwd+/etc/shadow backups on the same and peered devices; verify whether unauthorized config was pushed to edge devices.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage has "evil_tenant.csv"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, ProcessName, Facility, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Rogue root account 'troot' created on Cisco SD-WAN appliance AIInstallation High
Detects creation of the attacker's persistence account named troot with root (uid 0) privileges, the post-exploitation step of CVE-2026-20245. Catches the account-creation event even though attackers later attempt to delete it as an anti-forensic measure. Rationale: 'troot' is the exact rogue account name reported by Mandiant; pairing it with account-creation verbs / uid=0 isolates the persistence step from any benign mention of the string. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/zero-day-exploitation-cisco-catalyst-sd-wan-manager • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/cisco-catalyst-sd-wan-zero-day-cve-2026.html
ATT&CKT1136.001 T1078.003
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A real administrator who legitimately names a service account 'troot' (rare, but possible)
  • Red-team/BAS recreating the IOC to validate detection coverage
  • Configuration-management tooling templating a root-equivalent account with a matching name
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm whether a 'troot' (or any uid=0) account exists or was created-then-deleted on the appliance; review the creating session's source account and IP. Step 2 (contain): Remove the rogue account, rotate all local and vmanage-admin credentials, revoke device certificates, and block the source peer/IP at the management plane. Step 3 (hunt): Look for su pivots into troot, /etc/passwd+/etc/shadow backups, deletion of evil_tenant.csv, and the same account-creation pattern on peered controllers and edge devices.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage has "troot"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("useradd","adduser","new user","new account","/etc/passwd","uid=0","useradd[")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Privilege pivot via 'su' to rogue root account troot on SD-WAN device AIExploitation High
Detects the Linux su command being used to switch from the compromised administrative account to the newly created troot root account — the article's explicit privilege-escalation pivot. High fidelity because it correlates the su action with the attacker-specific target username. Rationale: The su->troot pivot is named directly by Mandiant; tying su to the unique target account troot removes the high volume of legitimate su-to-root noise. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/zero-day-exploitation-cisco-catalyst-sd-wan-manager • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/cisco-catalyst-sd-wan-zero-day-cve-2026.html

Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment

Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the originating account that ran su (likely the compromised admin/vmanage-admin) and the session source IP; pull the full shell history for that session. Step 2 (contain): Kill active troot sessions, disable/remove the account, rotate credentials and certificates, and isolate the device from peers/edges. Step 3 (hunt): Trace commands executed under troot (config exfiltration, edge-device config push, cleanup scripts) and check peered controllers for the same su pivot.

Bun runtime executing codfish/semantic-release-action index.js payload on CI runner AIInstallation High
Hunts the Miasma composite-action payload step on a GitHub Actions runner: the bun runtime invoked as 'bun run $GITHUB_ACTION_PATH/index.js' where the action path resolves to codfish/semantic-release-action. The legitimate v1 action was Docker-based (entrypoint.js) and never used bun, so bun executing index.js from this action's path is the compromise itself. Rationale: Anchors on bun + 'index.js' + 'semantic-release-action' from the article's verbatim composite-action step ('bun run $GITHUB_ACTION_PATH/index.js'); GITHUB_ACTION_PATH expands to the _actions/codfish/semantic-release-action path so both tokens co-occur in the cmdline. The original Docker action never used bun, making this combination malicious by construction. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/compromised-github-action-codfish-steals-secrets • https://x.com/step_security/status/2069831503471882383 • https://safedep.io/inside-the-miasma-supply-chain-attack-toolkit/
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer locally testing bun against a project that happens to have a file named index.js inside a directory named semantic-release-action
  • An internal fork/mirror of the action legitimately re-tooled to use bun for builds
  • Security researchers detonating the IOC in a sandboxed CI runner
  • A monorepo with an unrelated package literally named 'semantic-release-action' built with bun
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full ProcessCommandLine and parent chain — confirm parent is a GitHub Actions runner (Runner.Worker/bash) and the action path resolves to codfish/semantic-release-action; capture the runner host and the repo/workflow that triggered it. 2) Contain: cancel/disable the affected workflow, rotate every secret that workflow could touch (GITHUB_TOKEN is auto-scoped but rotate any NPM_TOKEN / PAT / cloud creds), and pin the action to a known-clean SHA (v1.0.0–v1.10.0 or v2.0.0). 3) Hunt: search all repos for references to codfish/semantic-release-action@v2–v5, look for the index.js SHA256 (UC2) and bun→api.github.com egress (UC3) on the same runner, and review npm publish logs for unauthorized releases.

| where ProcessCommandLine has "semantic-release-action"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine,
          ParentProcess = InitiatingProcessFileName, ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate

| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "semantic-release-action"

Known Miasma index.js payload hash present on CI runner (codfish action) AIDelivery High
Definitive IOC sweep for the byte-identical malicious index.js payload (sha256 9f93d77d...) dropped by the compromised codfish/semantic-release-action across DeviceFileEvents, DeviceProcessEvents and DeviceImageLoadEvents. Any host carrying this hash has pulled the trojanised action. Rationale: Uses the article's confirmed payload IOC (sha256 9f93d77d32833a515bc406c46da477142bb1ac2babeecb6aa42f98669a6db015, byte-identical across both malicious commits). A hash match is unambiguous, hence alerting. Sigma/Splunk/Datadog/Falcon left empty because file-write events on those stacks (Sysmon EID 11, CIM Endpoint.Filesystem, Falcon FileWritten) do not carry a SHA256 for a non-executed script file — the hash IOC only lives cleanly in Defender/ASIM file telemetry. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/compromised-github-action-codfish-steals-secrets • https://snyk.io/blog/miasma-supply-chain-attack-malicious-code-redhat-cloud-services-npm-packages/

  • An AV/EDR quarantine copy of the file retaining the original hash
  • A sandbox/detonation host where the sample was deliberately staged
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host is a CI runner and identify which workflow/repo pulled it; the InitiatingProcess shows whether bun executed it. 2) Contain: isolate the runner, kill the bun process tree, and rotate all secrets exposed to any workflow that ran on that runner (GITHUB_TOKEN scope, NPM_TOKEN with publish rights, cloud/CI PATs). 3) Hunt: enumerate every repo referencing codfish/semantic-release-action@v2/v2.2.1/v3*/v4*/v5*, repin to clean v1.x or v2.0.0, and check npm/registry audit logs for unexpected package publishes.

Bun process reaching GitHub commit-search API — Miasma dead-drop C2 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the Miasma infrastructure-less C2: the bun-run payload polls GitHub's public commit-search API (api.github.com) for marker-tagged commits whose body it passes to eval(). Outbound to GitHub initiated specifically by the bun runtime (the 'Cleanup Action' step) is the dead-drop resolver beacon, distinct from normal git/node CI traffic. Rationale: Anchors on the article's described C2 design (Miasma polls GitHub's public commit-search API and eval()s the matching commit body) plus the bun-run payload step; corroborated by The Register/SafeDep on the leaked toolkit. Scoping egress to bun (not git/node/curl) and the action cmdline separates the dead-drop beacon from normal CI traffic to GitHub. Sentinel left empty because no process-attributed egress table is available in this tenant (ASIM ImNetworkSession/ImWebSession lack initiating-process), so the bun-specific pivot needs Defender DeviceNetworkEvents. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/compromised-github-action-codfish-steals-secrets • https://www.theregister.com/cyber-crime/2026/06/09/miasma-supply-chain-attack-toolkit-goes-public-on-github/5253074 • https://safedep.io/inside-the-miasma-supply-chain-attack-toolkit/
ATT&CKT1102.001 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate bun-based CI step that genuinely calls the GitHub API (e.g. bun-native release tooling fetching releases)
  • A self-hosted runner where bun is the standard JS runtime and hits api.github.com for package metadata
  • DNS telemetry attributing the resolution to bun when a child git subprocess actually made the call
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "semantic-release-action"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the bun process that made the request was launched from the codfish/semantic-release-action path (correlate with UC1) and pull the resolved IP plus any url query if captured. 2) Contain: isolate the runner, block egress from runner subnets to api.github.com for non-allowlisted processes, and rotate secrets exposed to workflows on that runner. 3) Hunt: capture the bun process memory/handles for evidence of Runner.Worker access (secret theft), look for the index.js hash (UC2) on the host, and review GitHub commit-search-API access patterns from other runners for the same dead-drop behaviour.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("bun","bun.exe")
| where RemoteUrl has "github.com"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "index.js" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "semantic-release-action"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("bun","bun.exe")
| where RemoteUrl has "github.com"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "index.js" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "semantic-release-action"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Bun Runtime DNS Query to GitHub API (Miasma Dead-Drop C2)
id: b8e1d57c-3a92-4c0e-9f6d-71a4e2c8b903
description: Detects the bun runtime resolving github.com, consistent with the Miasma payload polling the GitHub commit-search API as an infrastructure-less dead-drop resolver.
references:
  - https://www.aikido.dev/blog/compromised-github-action-codfish-steals-secrets
  - https://www.theregister.com/cyber-crime/2026/06/09/miasma-supply-chain-attack-toolkit-goes-public-on-github/5253074
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/25
tags:
  - attack.t1102.001
  - attack.t1071.001
logsource:
  category: dns
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\bun.exe'
      - '/bun'
    QueryName|contains: 'github.com'
  condition: selection
level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @Image:(*\bun.exe OR */bun OR *\BUN.EXE) @DestinationHostname:*github.com*
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/github\.com$/i
| ContextImageFileName=/\/bun(\.exe)?$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, DomainName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where (All_Traffic.process_name="bun" OR All_Traffic.process_name="bun.exe") (All_Traffic.dest="*github.com*" OR All_Traffic.dest_host="*github.com*") by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.process_name All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_host All_Traffic.dest_port
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where (All_Traffic.process_name="bun" OR All_Traffic.process_name="bun.exe") (All_Traffic.dest="*github.com*" OR All_Traffic.dest_host="*github.com*") by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.process_name All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_host All_Traffic.dest_port
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Suspicious browser extension installation Installation Medium
Side-loaded / unsigned extensions, often masquerading as wallets, productivity tools.
ATT&CKT1176
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry DeviceRegistryEvents
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where RegistryKey has_any ("\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\","\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\","\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\")

                              @"\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\")
